justification_text:
At the one-day horizon, my point estimate of 61.3 was anchored heavily on the most recent observed price or level, with very little expected drift over such a short window. Short-term mean reversion tendencies and the absence of any imminent scheduled catalysts kept the estimate close to the prevailing value. The tight confidence interval of 59.5 to 63.1 reflects the relatively low realized volatility expected over a single trading session, where intraday noise is bounded and liquidity conditions tend to absorb small shocks without large directional moves.

At the one-week horizon, the point estimate nudges slightly higher to 61.8, reflecting a modest directional bias built into the underlying trend or carry structure I was modeling. The wider interval of 58.0 to 65.6 captures the accumulation of daily uncertainties compounding over five sessions, including the possibility of macro data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment meaningfully. A full week is long enough for a narrative shift to take hold in markets, so the tails need to be meaningfully fatter than at the daily horizon.

At the one-month horizon, the point estimate of 62.5 reflects a continuation of the gradual upward drift, though the very wide interval of 55.0 to 70.0 acknowledges that a month is a long time over which structural reassessments can occur. Monthly horizons are sensitive to regime changes — a shift in monetary policy expectations, a significant economic data surprise, or a geopolitical shock could easily push the outcome well outside the central scenario. The asymmetry in the interval is modest, but the overall width signals genuine humility about directional conviction.

Specific tail risks that could push outcomes outside even these stated intervals include a sudden liquidity crisis or flash crash on the downside, or an unexpected policy reversal or supply shock on the upside. Black swan events by definition are not well-captured in the 90% confidence interval, and correlation breakdowns during stress periods could amplify moves substantially. Model mis-specification — particularly if the volatility regime shifts or serial correlation in returns changes — represents a structural risk to the calibration of all three horizons simultaneously.
